ca_riverside_quarry.blurb: Riverside Quarry is a former quarry in the Inland Empire and the main sport destination around the city of Riverside. The rock is granite, with odd features left behind by the quarrying. Nearly all the climbing is bolted sport, usually over a hundred feet long, and many routes can be done with ten to twelve quickdraws; there are a few trad lines and a small bouldering section too. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.13, with the bulk between 5.10 and 5.12, so it suits strong climbers better than beginners. Most of the quarry faces west: in summer you can climb until about midday, and in winter the Agony Arch zone is best early with the rest of the crag later. Weekends are busy, but the many zones spread people out. Slab City, Roof Area and Torture Machine Area are among the larger zones.

az_superstition_mountains.blurb: The Superstition Mountains rise just east of the Phoenix metro area, and most of the range is designated wilderness, so the climbing feels remote and approaches can be long. The rock is volcanic and can be loose in places, though established routes are mostly on reasonably sound stone. Trad dominates, about four in five of the climbs, with a modest group of boulder problems and a few sport lines. Grades run from easy up to 5.11, mostly between 5.6 and 5.10. Barks Canyon Wall has several pleasant moderate multipitch lines. Miners Needle, The Cemetery, The Fortress and Wild Horse Wall are among the larger sub-areas, with Miners Needle a long hike in. Carry your own protection, since routes are traditional in nature, and test holds before trusting them.

ca_shangri_la_valley.blurb: Shangri-La Valley is the largest bouldering zone of the Tramway area, high in the San Jacinto Mountains near Palm Springs at around 8,400 to 8,500 feet. All of it is boulder problems on granite, and the style tends toward steep and featured. Difficulty covers a lot of ground, from very easy up to V12, with more than half the problems at V3 or easier and a solid middle at V4 to V7. The Beach is the biggest sub-area, a wide, mostly flat open space, with the Shangri-La zone, Dance Floor, Boardwalk Area and West Rim around it. Because of the altitude this is a warm-season place: the range is mostly a spring-through-fall destination, summer is the peak, and winter brings snow.

co_ophir.blurb: Ophir is a high-altitude climbing zone near Telluride, at about 8,500 feet, known for old-school, serious trad climbing with a sport side too. Roughly two thirds of the climbs are trad and one third sport, with grades from 5.7 to 5.13 concentrated between 5.9 and 5.12. Ophir Wall is the main cliff, with nearly a hundred routes up to about 600 feet on granitic rock, using a mix of gear and bolts. Cracked Canyon is mostly trad, offering rock climbing in summer and ice in winter. The Dark Side is the sport-heavy area, holding some of the harder bolted lines. Pack small gear and a steady head, since the style here is bold and multi-pitch.

ct_west_rock_state_park.blurb: West Rock State Park is a traprock ridge on Connecticut's Western Coastal Slope, with cliffs of dolerite rising several hundred feet. Bouldering makes up about three quarters of the climbs, with sport routes at the old quarry on the south end and some trad. The boulders of God's Country, roughly a hundred problems, are scattered along the base of the west-facing cliffs: solid, gritty rock with good friction, afternoon sun, and a remote feel high on the hillside. Boulder grades run from V0 to V8, mostly V0 to V3. South Buttress is mostly slab climbing apart from the quarry, with sport and trad from about 5.6 to 5.12. Both main areas face west and warm up on sunny days, which makes them good for cold-weather climbing.

id_dierkes_lake.blurb: Dierkes Lake sits in the Snake River canyon near Twin Falls, Idaho, with climbing on the cliffs around a small lake, reached by trails along the shore. The climbs split about evenly between bouldering and sport. The boulders are on basalt full of pockets, huecos, jugs, crimps and slopers, with problems from V0 to V7 and most between V0 and V4. The sport routes are steep and powerful, centered on the Alcove, whose big overhangs seldom allow onsights; grades mainly run 5.10 to 5.12, with a few moderates. Winter is the strongest season for the boulders, often the warmest choice in southern Idaho during the cold months. The Prow and North Shore are other larger sport sub-areas.
